title: Berkshire Hathaway Q2 Earnings Preview: Buybacks, Taylor Morrison, and the Abel Era's Report Card
excerpt: Berkshire is expected to report Saturday, with focus on up to $11 billion in share buybacks, Greg Abel's first major acquisition, and a $10 billion Alphabet bet.
body:
• Berkshire Hathaway is expected to report second-quarter earnings on Saturday, with investors focused on share buybacks that may have totaled $5 billion to $11 billion — a dramatic increase from $235 million in Q1.
  • New CEO Greg Abel's $6.8 billion acquisition of homebuilder Taylor Morrison during the quarter and the $10 billion investment in Alphabet's equity raise are the two biggest capital-deployment decisions of his tenure so far.
  • Wall Street estimates suggest Berkshire's earnings could fall about 3% year-over-year, but UBS analyst Brian Meredith projects a 3% gain driven by buybacks, higher BNSF railroad earnings, and lower catastrophe losses in insurance.

Berkshire Hathaway is set to report its second-quarter earnings at 8 a.m. ET on Saturday, delivering what amounts to the most comprehensive scorecard yet of CEO Greg Abel's performance since he took the reins from Warren Buffett on January 1.

The report will arrive with Berkshire's Class B shares trading around $519, up more than 10% since June but still trailing the S&P 500's roughly 14% total return for the year. Class A shares closed Wednesday at $777,696.

The Buyback Question

Share repurchases are likely to dominate the narrative. A July securities filing by 95-year-old Chairman Buffett indicated that Berkshire's Class A share count declined by around 11,000 between mid-April and mid-July, suggesting between $5 billion and $11 billion in buybacks during the quarter, according to Barron's analysis.

That would represent a massive acceleration from the $235 million Berkshire repurchased in the first quarter — which itself was the first buyback since May 2024. UBS analysts estimate the figure at $8.5 billion and have raised their price target for Class B shares to $585 from $570, calling the buyback activity a bullish signal.

"Greg did that faster than I could [have] done it, smoother than I could have done it, and I never talked to the CEO. He has launched."

— Warren Buffett on Abel's Taylor Morrison acquisition, to CNBC

Abel's Big Moves

Beyond buybacks, two major capital-deployment decisions will be under scrutiny. In the second quarter, Berkshire completed its $6.8 billion acquisition of homebuilder Taylor Morrison — Abel's first major deal and a significant bet on America's housing market. Buffett publicly endorsed the move, telling CNBC that Abel executed it better than he could have.

Berkshire also invested $10 billion in Google parent Alphabet's $85 billion equity capital raise in June, purchasing shares at below $350 each. Alphabet stock has since risen to around $360, giving Berkshire a quick paper gain on the position. Buffett told CNBC he initiated the investment.

Earnings Outlook

Wall Street consensus calls for earnings of about $7,553 per Class A share and roughly $5 per Class B share, a 3% decline year-over-year, according to FactSet. But UBS analyst Brian Meredith — who has a strong track record on Berkshire predictions — projects a 3% gain to nearly $8,000 per Class A share, citing higher BNSF railroad earnings and lower catastrophe losses in Berkshire's insurance businesses.

Investors will also watch Berkshire's cash levels closely. The company's cash pile hit a record $397 billion in Q1, but the Alphabet investment and Taylor Morrison acquisition likely drew it down in Q2. The 10-Q filing, expected alongside earnings, will detail equity purchases and sales but probably not name specific securities — those will come in Berkshire's 13-F filing on August 14.

What's at Stake

The Abel era at Berkshire is taking shape as "continuity with a harder edge," as Motley Fool analysts have described it. Berkshire trades at roughly 1.4 times book value — at the lower end of its recent historical range — and about 15 times earnings. Neither cheap nor expensive, but backed by a war chest, a portfolio of durable operating businesses, and a new CEO who has demonstrated willingness to act quickly. Saturday's report will show whether that combination is producing results.
